data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["A perturbation test in code execution is deterministic and universal; in human judgment, 'equivalent' perturbations are subjective and may introduce confounds.","Code either crashes or runs; human panels exhibit graded disagreement, making the threshold for 'detection' ambiguous."],"overturn_conditions":["The domain expert's intuition is demonstrably superior on items where the checklist is silent or misleading.","The non-expert panel cannot reliably perform the feature-detection step the checklist demands.","No checklist-equivalent perturbation can be constructed that is both valid and discriminating within a single evaluation."],"shared_structure":["Both involve a structured process (checklist/rule) intended to ensure reliable outcomes.","Both can suffer from a decoupling of process-adherence from genuine validity (mere compliance vs. cargo culting).","Both require a perturbation test to distinguish genuine understanding from procedural mimicry."],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_001","SRC_002","SRC_005"],"transfer_claims":["The core transferable principle is that genuine reliability is sensitive to the *validity* of the inputs, not just their *format*. A perturbation that maintains the format but violates the validity exposes procedural mimicry.","The 'cargo cult' diagnostic applies directly: a panel that reaches the right answer for the wrong (procedural) reasons will fail when the procedural shortcut is exploited."]},"claim":"A trained non-expert panel using an explicit checklist will produce more reliable judgments on tasks with verifiable outcomes because the checklist externalizes the critical feature-detection step into an interpretable, auditable format, and aggregation averages out residual noise. Genuine reliability is distinguished from mere compliance by introducing targeted checklist-equivalent perturbations: substituting a superficially similar but decision-irrelevant feature for a genuine one. A panel showing genuine reliability will exhibit higher disagreement and error rates on perturbed items, whereas mere compliance will blindly follow the checklist to the same 'correct' answer, failing to register that the evidential basis has changed.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The checklist is poorly designed and omits a critical feature that expert intuition reliably captures.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The task involves high-order feature interaction where the rules of combination are tacit and cannot be externalized into a linear checklist.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The perturbation is not truly equivalent in the eyes of the checklist, meaning it fails to isolate mere compliance from genuine semantic processing.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"The non-expert panel is not truly independent, introducing correlated errors (e.g., shared training biases) that the aggregation cannot average out.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The checklist transforms an ill-posed holistic judgment into a structured, multi-step algorithm. Non-experts act as feature detectors and rule appliers. Their independence ensures independent errors (e.g., lapses in attention) average out, while the checklist ensures the signal (critical features) is consistently extracted. The perturbation mechanism works because genuine reliability depends on the *validity* of the underlying features. If a panel's accuracy is merely procedural, it will treat a 'fake' feature that passes the checklist's formal criteria as a real one. If the reliability is genuine, the panel's underlying semantic processing will detect the anomaly, causing disagreement or an accuracy drop.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
